A fritter is a piece of food — fruit, vegetable, meat, seafood, or almost anything — that is coated in a thick, wet batter and then deep-fried in hot oil.

That's the heart of it. A fritter is not just fried food. The defining feature is the batter coating — that wet, doughy mixture (usually made of flour, egg, and milk) that wraps around the food before it hits the oil. When fried, this coating puffs up and turns into a crispy, golden-brown crust on the outside, while the food inside becomes soft and cooked through.

Almost anything can become a fritter. The filling is what gives each type of fritter its name:

  • Apple fritter — chunks of apple inside a sweet batter, often dusted with powdered sugar or glazed. This is one of the most well-known types, common as a pastry or doughnut in bakeries.
  • Corn fritter — sweet corn mixed into the batter and fried in small rounds, popular in American and Southern cooking.
  • Banana fritter — slices of banana dipped in batter and fried, very common across Asian cuisines.
  • Vegetable fritter — vegetables like zucchini, onion, or spinach mixed or coated in batter and fried.
  • Prawn/shrimp fritter — whole prawns coated in batter and deep-fried.
  • Clam fritter — clams mixed into batter and fried, popular in coastal American regions.

The pattern is always the same: something + batter + hot oil = fritter.
What a Fritter Looks and Feels Like

A fritter is typically small and round or roughly oval in shape, though it doesn't have to be perfectly shaped. The outside is crispy and a little rough or lumpy because the batter doesn't form a perfectly smooth shell — it bubbles and sets unevenly in the oil, which is part of its charm.

Bite into one and you get a contrast: the crunch of the fried crust gives way to the soft, moist filling inside. This texture contrast — crunchy outside, tender inside — is what makes fritters so enjoyable to eat.

They are almost always served hot, right after frying, because the crispiness fades as they cool and the crust turns soft.
How Fritters Differ from Similar Foods

People sometimes confuse fritters with other fried foods. Here's how to keep them distinct:

  • A doughnut is made from a dough (thicker and firmer than batter) that is shaped and then fried. An apple fritter from a doughnut shop is a close cousin of a doughnut — it uses a similar enriched dough — but the classic fritter tradition uses a thinner, wetter batter poured or dipped over a filling.
  • A tempura (from Japanese cooking) is also batter-fried food, but tempura batter is deliberately light, thin, and airy, giving a delicate coating. Fritter batter is thicker and heartier, producing a chunkier, more substantial crust.
  • A pakora (from South Asian cooking) is the regional equivalent of a fritter — vegetables dipped in a spiced chickpea batter and fried. In everyday terms, a pakora is a fritter, just under a different cultural name.
  • Breaded fried food (like a breaded chicken cutlet) uses dry breadcrumbs, not a wet batter. Fritters always involve a wet batter.

One of the most interesting things about fritters is that nearly every cuisine in the world has its own version, because the method (coat in batter, fry in oil) is universally simple and produces delicious results.

  • In Spain and Latin America, buñuelos are fried dough fritters, sometimes stuffed with cheese or sweet fillings.
  • In West Africa and the Caribbean, accara or akara are fritters made from black-eyed peas.
  • In Indonesia and Malaysia, bakwan are vegetable fritters.
  • In Italy, frittelle are sweet fritters eaten during festivals.
  • In India, the pakora is everywhere — onion pakora, paneer pakora, chilli pakora.

The word and the food are deeply embedded in global culinary culture.

• She bought an apple fritter from the bakery and ate it with her morning coffee.
  • The stall was selling prawn fritters wrapped in newspaper.
  • He had never tried a corn fritter until he visited the Southern United States.
  • The menu listed a basket of vegetable fritters as a starter.

A fritter is a small, deep-fried food made by coating fruit, vegetables, meat, or seafood in a thick batter and frying it until the outside is crispy and golden while the inside remains soft — a simple, universally loved method of cooking found in cuisines all over the world.
